claims.text: Rapidly deposited HEA coatings can have a nanocrystalline, single-phase solid-solution microstructure.
The wear resistance of HEA protective coatings is governed primarily by nanocrystalline grain size and the associated high grain-boundary density.
Rapid solidification creates a high density of grain boundaries in these coatings.
A high density of grain boundaries hinders localized shear-band formation and propagation during sliding wear.
A high density of grain boundaries hinders crack propagation during sliding wear.
Sub-solidus annealing can systematically coarsen the coating grains without changing the overall composition.
Grain coarsening lowers grain-boundary density and thereby reduces barriers to localized plastic deformation and crack propagation.
Annealed, coarser-grained coatings will have higher wear volume loss than otherwise comparable as-deposited nanocrystalline coatings.
As-deposited fine-grained coatings may have a lower friction coefficient than annealed, coarser-grained coatings.
The proposed grain-boundary effect should be observable over an approximately 10–100 nm grain-size range.
The hypothesis should apply to coatings of comparable composition and similar nanocrystalline as-deposited microstructure.
Significant oxide-scale formation may dominate wear and limit the applicability of the proposed grain-boundary mechanism.
Dynamic oxidation or phase transformations could contribute to the observed wear performance.

contradictions.description: A lower friction coefficient is presented only as a potential outcome, but the falsification rule can be read as treating the absence of a significant friction increase after annealing as sufficient to falsify the hypothesis. This is stronger than the stated prediction and could reject the hypothesis even if the predicted wear-volume increase occurs.
